headline: NCAA Women’s Lacrosse Committees Propose Simpler Penalties
dek: The package would make every yellow card a two-minute non-releasable penalty, add targeting as a red-card foul and broaden video review.
entities: Division I Women’s Lacrosse Rules Subcommittee
Division II and III Women’s Lacrosse Rules Committee

sources.title: Simplified penalty structure recommended in women’s lacrosse

lead.creator: c w
lead.rightsBasis: CC0 public-domain dedication documented on Wikimedia Commons and verified against the Flickr-origin rights record.
lead.caption: Christopher Newport and York College players compete in a 2014 women’s lacrosse match. NCAA committees have proposed a simplified penalty structure for 2026-27.
lead.alt: Women’s college lacrosse players contest the ball during a match.

charts.caption: The proposal would make every yellow card a two-minute non-releasable penalty and classify targeting as a red-card foul.
charts.alt: Graphic lists a two-minute non-releasable yellow-card penalty and a targeting red-card foul.

charts.caption: Fall experiments include a 60-second possession clock after draws, 11-player lineups and a backcourt-style rule.
charts.alt: Graphic lists a 60-second possession clock, 11-player lineups and a backcourt experiment.

paragraphs: NCAA women’s lacrosse rules committees have proposed a simplified penalty system for the 2026-27 academic year, but the package is not yet official and still requires oversight approval.

The proposal would make every yellow card a two-minute, non-releasable penalty. Committees said the change is meant to match punishment more closely to the severity of a foul and improve consistency, safety and game administration.

Existing stick and body-contact fouls would be consolidated into clearer illegal-check and illegal-contact categories. Flopping would become a flagrant foul carrying a yellow card, while a new targeting foul would carry a red card.

The proposed targeting definition covers forcible contact made without a legitimate attempt to play the ball when the primary purpose is a hit with high potential for injury. A red card would still eject a player, but the automatic next-game suspension would be removed.

Video review requests would be limited to coaches, and officials would be directed to try to finish a review within two minutes. Reviews could also identify the correct offender whenever a card is administered.
Timing limits would apply: after a goal, an eligible request would have to arrive before the draw clock expires; during a timeout, it would have to be made in the first 30 seconds.
Other proposals include one stick check per quarter for players taking draws, stopping both clocks during official warnings and allowing an on-field stick exchange when neither player has the ball.

Fall experiments would test a 60-second possession clock after a draw instead of 90 seconds, reduce lineups from 12 players to 11 and try a backcourt-style restriction after the offense advances below the restraining line.

The committees’ recommendations are only one step in the rules process. The NCAA said all proposals must be approved before they become official, so teams should distinguish the published proposal from the eventual rulebook.
facts: The proposals are intended for the 2026-27 academic year if approved.
Every yellow card would carry a two-minute non-releasable penalty.
Targeting would be a new flagrant foul carrying a red card.
Fall experiments would test a 60-second possession clock, 11-player lineups and a backcourt-style rule.
uncertainty: The recommendations were not official rules when the NCAA published them.
Oversight panels may approve, reject or modify individual proposals.
seoTitle: NCAA women’s lacrosse penalty rules proposed for 2026-27
seoDescription: NCAA committees propose two-minute yellow cards, a targeting red card and broader video review for women’s lacrosse.

headline: FDA Approves First Regulatory T-Cell Therapy for Stem-Cell Transplants
dek: Tregzi improved one-year chronic GVHD-free survival to 78% in a randomized trial of 187 adults, compared with 38.4% after a standard transplant.

sources.title: FDA Approves New Treatment That Uses Donor Immune Cells to Prevent Serious Complications in Blood Cancer Patients

lead.creator: Bill Branson
lead.rightsBasis: National Cancer Institute photograph documented as U.S. government public domain and unrestricted for reuse on Wikimedia Commons.
lead.attribution: Bill Branson / National Cancer Institute, public domain
lead.caption: Scientists work in a National Cancer Institute basic research laboratory. FDA approved Tregzi, the first regulatory T-cell-based immunotherapy for a stem-cell transplant indication.
lead.alt: Three scientists work among benches and equipment in a cancer research laboratory.

charts.caption: At one year, chronic GVHD-free survival was 78% with Tregzi and 38.4% with a standard transplant in PRECISION-T.
charts.alt: Graphic compares 78 percent with Tregzi and 38.4 percent with standard transplant.

charts.caption: After accounting for death as a competing risk, serious chronic GVHD within one year occurred in 12.6% of Tregzi recipients and 44% of controls.
charts.alt: Graphic compares serious chronic GVHD rates of 12.6 percent and 44 percent.

paragraphs: The Food and Drug Administration approved Tregzi as the first regulatory T-cell-based immunotherapy for improving chronic graft-versus-host-disease-free survival in adults with blood cancers receiving a matched-donor stem-cell transplant.

Tregzi combines blood-forming stem and progenitor cells with selected donor immune cells. The aim is to rebuild blood and immune systems while lowering the risk that donor cells attack the recipient’s body after transplantation.

Approval rested on PRECISION-T, a multicenter, open-label randomized trial involving 187 adults with acute leukemia or myelodysplastic syndrome. Ninety-three received Tregzi and 94 received an unmanipulated allograft.
At one year, 78% of Tregzi recipients were alive without moderate or severe chronic graft-versus-host disease, compared with 38.4% in the standard-transplant group, FDA reported.

After accounting for death as a competing risk, 12.6% of Tregzi recipients developed serious chronic graft-versus-host disease within one year, compared with 44% of patients receiving a standard transplant.

Infections were the most common side effects and were generally consistent with the risks expected after stem-cell transplantation. FDA reported no severe infusion reactions and no graft failures during the study period.

The indication is specific: matched-donor transplantation with a myeloablative preparative regimen for adults with hematologic malignancies. It does not establish that the product is appropriate for every patient or transplant setting.
FDA granted the application Orphan Drug and Regenerative Medicine Advanced Therapy designations and approved the product for Orca Biosystems.

The randomized results establish a benefit in the approved population, but longer follow-up, real-world use and the full prescribing information remain important for understanding durability and uncommon risks.
facts: FDA approved Tregzi on June 30, 2026.
PRECISION-T randomized 187 adults.
One-year chronic GVHD-free survival was 78% with Tregzi and 38.4% with standard transplant.
Serious chronic GVHD within one year was 12.6% versus 44% after accounting for death as a competing risk.
uncertainty: Trial results apply to the studied matched-donor, myeloablative transplant population.
The approval record does not eliminate the need for longer-term safety and effectiveness follow-up.
seoTitle: FDA approves Tregzi, first regulatory T-cell transplant therapy
seoDescription: FDA approved Tregzi after a 187-patient trial found higher one-year chronic GVHD-free survival than standard transplant.

headline: National Recording Registry Adds 25 Works, Reaching 700
dek: The 2026 class spans 70 years and includes first registry selections for Beyoncé and Taylor Swift, but the Library does not hold every listed recording.

lead.creator: Architect of the Capitol
lead.rightsBasis: Official Architect of the Capitol photograph documented as U.S. federal-government public domain on Wikimedia Commons; news use is within the source’s stated permitted purposes.
lead.attribution: Architect of the Capitol, public domain
lead.caption: The Library of Congress Packard Campus for Audio-Visual Conservation in Culpeper, Virginia. The National Recording Registry reached 700 entries with its 2026 class.
lead.alt: The Packard Campus conservation center sits amid green lawns below a wooded hillside.

charts.caption: The 2026 National Recording Registry class added 25 recordings spanning 70 years.
charts.alt: Graphic shows 25 recordings spanning 70 years in the 2026 registry class.

charts.caption: The 2026 additions brought the registry to 700 entries, roughly 0.01% of the Library’s four million collected recordings.
charts.alt: Graphic shows 700 registry entries and four million recordings in the Library’s collection.

paragraphs: The Library of Congress added 25 recordings to the National Recording Registry in 2026, bringing the preservation list to 700 entries.
This year’s class spans 70 years of music, news, sports broadcasts and other recorded sound, from Spike Jones and His City Slickers’ 1944 single “Cocktails for Two” to works released in the 2010s.

Beyoncé’s “Single Ladies (Put a Ring on It)” and Taylor Swift’s album “1989” became the first registry selections for each artist. Weezer’s self-titled debut and José Feliciano’s “Feliz Navidad” also joined the list.
The Go-Go’s album “Beauty and the Beat,” Rosanne Cash’s “The Wheel” and the original Broadway cast recording of “Chicago” are among the other selections.

Congress created the registry to recognize sound recordings that are culturally, historically or aesthetically significant and at least 10 years old. Selection supports preservation planning; it is not a ranking of artistic merit.

The Library said it received more than 3,000 public nominations. Public input informs the process, while the Librarian of Congress makes selections after consulting the National Recording Preservation Board.
The registry’s 700 entries represent about 0.01% of the Library’s collection of four million recordings, according to the Library’s announcement.

A registry entry does not necessarily mean the physical recording is stored in Washington or Culpeper. The Library says the national list includes works held in collections around the country and it does not currently possess every selection.

Preservation work can involve locating the best surviving source, stabilizing fragile media, making preservation copies and documenting the recording so it remains accessible as formats and playback equipment change.
facts: The 2026 class added 25 recordings on May 14, 2026.
The registry now contains 700 entries.
The class spans 70 years.
The Library received more than 3,000 public nominations.
uncertainty: Registry inclusion does not mean the Library holds a copy of every selection.
Selection recognizes preservation significance and is not an exhaustive measure of influence or quality.
seoTitle: 2026 National Recording Registry adds 25 works, reaches 700
seoDescription: The National Recording Registry’s 2026 class adds 25 recordings spanning 70 years and brings the preservation list to 700.

headline: IMF Sees Cambodia Growth Slowing to 3% as Inflation Rises
dek: Staff project 5.6% inflation in 2026 and warn that energy prices, weak tourism, real-estate stress and trade uncertainty tilt risks to the downside.

sources.title: IMF Staff Completes 2026 Article IV Mission to Cambodia

lead.creator: Mao Piseth
lead.rightsBasis: Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 license documented on Wikimedia Commons; citywide editorial crop does not isolate a protected architectural work.
lead.attribution: Mao Piseth / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0
lead.caption: Phnom Penh’s skyline and Royal Palace area in 2022. IMF staff project Cambodia’s economic growth will slow to 3% in 2026.
lead.alt: The Phnom Penh skyline stretches beyond the Royal Palace and riverfront under a hazy sky.

charts.caption: IMF staff estimate Cambodia’s real GDP growth slowed from 6% in 2024 to 5.3% in 2025 and project 3% in 2026.
charts.alt: Graphic shows Cambodia growth at 6 percent in 2024, 5.3 percent in 2025 and 3 percent in 2026.

charts.caption: IMF staff project 5.6% average inflation in 2026 and describe international reserves as adequate at about eight months of imports.
charts.alt: Graphic shows 5.6 percent projected inflation and about eight months of import reserves.

paragraphs: Cambodia’s economic growth is projected to slow to 3% in 2026 while average inflation rises to 5.6%, International Monetary Fund staff said after an Article IV consultation mission.

The preliminary estimate follows real GDP growth of 6% in 2024 and 5.3% in 2025. IMF staff cited higher energy prices, softer external demand, weak tourism, subdued domestic demand and trade-policy uncertainty.
Inflation averaged 2.5% in 2025 but rose sharply in May 2026. Staff expect the higher energy-cost pass-through to lift the annual average before inflation moderates in 2027.

The current account moved from a small surplus to a deficit in 2025 as imports outpaced still-strong exports and remittances declined. Foreign direct investment remained strong, and reserves were assessed as adequate at about eight months of imports.

Risks are tilted downward for growth and upward for inflation. The IMF listed volatile energy prices, El Niño effects, trade uncertainty, weaker tourism, real-estate weakness and deteriorating asset quality among the threats.

Staff recommended temporary, targeted help for vulnerable households and affected firms while unwinding broad fuel support as price pressures ease. They also called for stronger tax compliance and tighter management of exemptions.

Cambodia’s broadly stable riel-dollar exchange rate remains a nominal anchor in a highly dollarized economy. The IMF urged agile liquidity management and stronger interbank markets as part of gradual de-dollarization.

The National Bank of Cambodia ended broad regulatory forbearance, which the IMF called an important step. Staff said banks should recognize losses promptly and maintain adequate provisions, especially given real-estate exposure.

These figures are staff’s preliminary mission findings, not a final Executive Board conclusion. A report remains subject to management approval and later Board discussion, and actual outcomes can change with energy prices, tourism, trade and domestic financial conditions.
facts: IMF staff project 3% real GDP growth in 2026.
Staff project 5.6% average inflation in 2026.
Growth slowed from 6% in 2024 to 5.3% in 2025.
International reserves were assessed at about eight months of imports.
uncertainty: The statement contains preliminary IMF staff findings, not a final Executive Board conclusion.
Growth and inflation forecasts are sensitive to energy prices, tourism, trade policy and financial-sector conditions.
seoTitle: Cambodia growth seen at 3% in 2026 as inflation rises: IMF
seoDescription: IMF staff project Cambodia growth slowing to 3% and inflation rising to 5.6% in 2026, with risks tilted to the downside.

headline: Most 401(k)s Do Not Require Spousal Consent for Withdrawals
dek: GAO found about one in 10 married households with a 401(k)-type account removed funds in 2021, while broader consent rules could add cost and delay.

sources.title: Retirement Security: Most Defined Contribution Plans Do Not Require Spousal Consent to Remove Funds and Doing So Would Involve Trade-offs

lead.creator: Shixart1985
lead.rightsBasis: Creative Commons Attribution 2.0 license documented on Wikimedia Commons.
lead.caption: An older couple reads together at home. GAO says most defined-contribution plans do not require a spouse’s consent before money is removed.
lead.alt: An older couple sits closely together reading a book at home.

charts.caption: About one in 10 married households with a 401(k)-type account removed funds in 2021, typically less than 10% of the household retirement balance.
charts.alt: Graphic shows one in 10 households removed funds and typically took less than 10 percent of the retirement balance.

charts.caption: Money-purchase and target-benefit plans subject to federal removal-consent rules accounted for less than 1% of private defined-contribution plans in 2022.
charts.alt: Graphic shows less than one percent of private defined-contribution plans in covered plan types.

paragraphs: Most private defined-contribution retirement plans, including most 401(k)s, do not require a married participant to obtain a spouse’s consent before taking a loan, withdrawal or distribution, the Government Accountability Office found.
Federal law generally protects a spouse as the default beneficiary and often requires consent to name someone else, but rules for actively removing money differ by plan design.
Money-purchase and target-benefit plans require consent for active fund removal, yet together they represented less than 1% of private-sector defined-contribution plans in 2022, GAO reported.

Using the Federal Reserve’s 2022 Survey of Consumer Finances, auditors estimated that about one in 10 married households with a 401(k)-type account removed funds in 2021. Those households typically took less than 10% of their total retirement balance.
The survey does not show whether a spouse knew about or agreed to a withdrawal. GAO said there are no nationally representative data measuring removals made without spousal knowledge.
Stakeholders told auditors such undisclosed withdrawals were likely uncommon, but the documented cases could cause severe losses, marital conflict and less time to rebuild savings before retirement.

Requiring consent across more plans could stop unilateral withdrawals, including during a divorce, but plan sponsors and record keepers said it could also raise administrative costs and delay emergency access to money.

Alternatives include notifying spouses, requiring consent only above a threshold or creating exceptions for circumstances such as domestic violence. GAO presented trade-offs rather than recommending one universal design.

For households, the immediate takeaway is structural rather than personal financial advice: beneficiary protections do not necessarily prevent money from leaving a 401(k), and the applicable rule depends on the plan.
facts: Most private defined-contribution plans do not require spousal consent for active fund removal.
Covered money-purchase and target-benefit plans were less than 1% of private defined-contribution plans in 2022.
About one in 10 married households with a 401(k)-type account removed funds in 2021.
Those households typically removed less than 10% of the total retirement balance.
uncertainty: National survey data do not show whether spouses knew about or agreed to withdrawals.
GAO did not recommend a single nationwide consent design and documented both protections and administrative trade-offs.
seoTitle: Most 401(k)s lack spousal consent rules for withdrawals: GAO
seoDescription: GAO says most 401(k)s do not require spousal consent for withdrawals, while broader protections could add costs and delays.

headline: Pentagon’s New 2028 Audit Strategy Leaves Key Risks Unresolved
dek: GAO says centralized testing of material balances may advance a clean opinion, but DOD would defer some internal-control fixes for at least two years.

sources.title: DOD Financial Management: Questions Associated with New Financial Audit Approach

lead.creator: Alexander Kubitza
lead.rightsBasis: Official Department of Defense photograph documented as U.S. government public domain on Wikimedia Commons.
lead.attribution: Alexander Kubitza / U.S. Department of Defense, public domain
lead.caption: The Pentagon in Arlington, Virginia, in 2023. GAO says DOD’s revised plan for a clean audit by 2028 leaves questions about controls, staffing and sustainability.
lead.alt: An aerial view shows the five-sided Pentagon complex and surrounding roads.

charts.caption: DOD’s revised audit strategy shifts from decentralized control remediation toward centralized coordination and evidence for material balances.
charts.alt: Graphic contrasts decentralized control remediation with centralized testing of material balances.

charts.caption: DOD spends more than $1 trillion annually and accounts for about 82% of federal physical assets, according to GAO testimony.
charts.alt: Graphic shows more than one trillion dollars in annual spending and 82 percent of federal physical assets.

paragraphs: The Defense Department’s revised plan to obtain a clean financial audit by the end of 2028 may sharpen attention on material account balances, but it leaves unresolved questions about internal controls, technology, fraud risk and workforce capacity, GAO testified.

DOD has never received an unmodified opinion on its department-wide financial statements. The inspector general issued a disclaimer for fiscal 2025 because auditors could not obtain enough evidence to form an opinion.

The new approach centralizes coordination, focuses on material line items and relies more on manual testing of large samples, with artificial-intelligence tools used as needed. The earlier approach emphasized decentralized remediation of control deficiencies.

GAO called the renewed focus encouraging but warned that DOD would not prioritize some key internal-control deficiencies for at least two years. Reliable controls matter beyond the audit because they support timely information for spending and operational decisions.

The department has undergone full-scope audits for eight years, and auditors have issued thousands of findings and recommendations over three decades. The Marine Corps first received a clean opinion for fiscal 2023 and has maintained one since.

Questions remain about transparent tracking of remediation, major information-technology weaknesses, fraud risks, trained financial-management staff and whether the new process will remain sustainable after 2028.

The scale makes the accounting problem consequential. GAO said DOD spends more than $1 trillion annually, represents almost half of federal discretionary spending and controls about 82% of federal physical assets.

Financial audits have already produced benefits including cost savings and avoidance, better systems and improved visibility into assets and inventory. Those gains do not amount to a clean department-wide opinion.

The 2028 date is a department goal, not an audit result. Success will depend on evidence tested by independent auditors and on whether DOD can address material balances without allowing the underlying control environment to deteriorate.
facts: DOD has never received a clean department-wide audit opinion.
The fiscal 2025 statements received a disclaimer of opinion.
The revised approach targets a clean opinion by the end of 2028.
GAO said DOD spends more than $1 trillion annually and controls about 82% of federal physical assets.
uncertainty: The 2028 clean-audit date is a DOD goal, not a verified outcome.
GAO’s testimony evaluates risks and questions in the strategy; future audit evidence will determine whether it succeeds.
seoTitle: GAO: Pentagon’s new 2028 clean-audit strategy leaves risks
seoDescription: GAO says DOD’s centralized 2028 audit strategy may help test material balances but leaves control, technology and staffing risks.
